## Design

### 2026-10-06 – Day 1: I Started My Research and Created My First PCB Draft!!!

**2h**

Day 1: I Started My Research and Created My First PCB Draft!!!

Today, I started working on my PCB idea: an alarm clock that runs away from you. I got this idea from a MrWhosTheBoss video in which he saw an alarm clock that ran away from you to get you up and running in the morning.

Part 1: Extensions
I decided to start by looking at what my project would consist of. Basically, it can be boiled down to 3 functions.
1) Producing an awakening obnoxious noise
2) Registering the loud noise
3) "Running" away

To take care of producing the loud noise, I decided to use a 5V Piezo Buzzer. It is quite cheap, often going for less than a buck, and is easy to control, as well as integrate into a PCB.

To detect the loud noise, I will use this sound sensor module, the KY-037 High-Sensitivity Microphone Sensor Module, which has good pricing at 2-3 dollars and very good frequency detection.

To make it run, I will use the TB6612FNG Dual Driver with N20 Micro Metal Gear Motors. The cost will be around $10 in total with tax. This is a splurge, but also the most functional part of the robot that code can't fix.

Part 2: PCB
Then, I switched over to the PCB. For the PCB, I needed:
1)  a microcontroller
2) a clock to keep track of time
3) a button for turning off the alarm
4) RESISTORS, so my PCB doesn't set off my fire alarm

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 204451](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/433e7ec67a2a2be2528235681685da88781b9ea288265486f7e00e229c686931.png)
For the microcontroller, I went with the ATmega328P-PU, which is a simple and cheap microcontroller to integrate into the PCB. Then I realized that getting an ATmega328P-PU DIP-28 is better because it will be like a plug-in extension for my ATmega microcontroller to take in and out.

For the inner clock, I went with the CSTCE16M0V53-R0, which is a 16V Ceramic Resonator. This keeps the microcontroller aware of the time from the start of the program. It is relatively cheap and very efficient, so I will solder it directly onto my PCB.

For the button, I decided to go with a regular tactile button, and for the resistor, I will just use a regular 10 Ohms resistor.

Part 3: PCB Schematic
This is the section that took me the longest. I had to watch over 3 videos on how to use online PCB schematic software before finally deciding on EasyEDA.

I watched my first video on how to use the interface. In it, I learned about the parts and libraries, along with the LCSC parts ordering partnership. Then, I started working on my design, and this is about as far as I got because I couldn't find some of the exact parts I wanted in the libraries, so I will have to make them myself.

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 203951](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/6c960141018dfdc17daf60cf61c3610e4d9400b5a509851fc8991658fdbc2591.png)

And that's about all I got done!

Time Spent: 2 hours

### 2026-10-08 – Day 2: Finish up my PCB schematic!

**3h**

Day 2: Finish up my PCB schematic!

Today I finally finished my PCB!

![Screenshot 2026-10-08 183900](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/b6f2aa57c013d8f72435f7360f9f08e303c693646d693c70a1d98de27e422fef.png)

This PCB is much improved from my Version 1 from yesterday. This PCB contains a microcontroller unit, sound  control (more on that later), motor control (also more on that later), and quite a few capacitors so the circuit does not fry up the second it is connected to a power source.

Part 1: Clarifications
In my Day 1 report, I should have been much more thorough about how my board will work and its connections.  Today, I will go more into the depths of the project.

Matter #1. My board is NOT optimized to solder directly to my modules, like sound and motor. I am a beginner; therefore, I do not trust myself to correctly solder the more expensive modules to a PCB and do it right. Instead, for all modules (and the Microcontroller), I will have a panel of 1 by x number of male pin connectors to hook up to the banded female wires/ribbon cables that go to corresponding male pins on these modules.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/0f1ff76850c1002a2fbf3c3f388fefc8a8a959a819d28ebf78224b9e6f0427e1.png)

Matter #2. THE DETAILS:
Last I checked, I only outlined those parts and the basic functionality of my design. We are going to change that by showing the connections between different parts and pieces in my project. PS. I did my deep research into this stuff today, so my writing might be a bit fried

First off, the microcontroller. The microcontroller is going to serve as the main command, with almost all parts linking to it in some way or another. The ATmega328P microcontroller that I chose is a very good option because of its dirt-cheap price, along with a multitude of pins and good quality. I will not go over all of the connections to it, but I connect it to the button and resistor sequence, sound module, and motor driving units.

Next, the clock/16mHz ceramic resonator is going to be necessary for my project because it is one based on time, and this part keeps track of time. It is only connected to the microcontroller.

The button and resistor unit is there to turn off the alarm, a necessary part to ensure that I don't get worse hearing. It is only connected to the board and each other; though important to note, it is connected to the RESET pin, an important part of the build.

The sound module is the part of the build the user interacts with the most, so I splurged and went for the KY-037, which allows for more complicated algorithms to be built, like detecting different frequencies and sounds, instead of blaring at any sound it hears. It is connected to the microcontroller and the battery unit.

My motor units are actually split up into 2 sections: the driver and the output headers. The motor drivers help connect the motor to communicate with the microcontroller without frying itself. I went with the MX1508, which had MOSFETS in it to easily make efficient use of the motors. The output headers and just a screw-wire connection, so I added those in; however, I am not fully convinced about which motor output module I should use, so that will remain unknown until I figure it out.

Finally, the battery pack is going to be 4 AA batteries. This will be connected up to my screw terminal (connected to the microcontroller VCC, then that to anything that needs power) and then to my step converter, which will knock back the voltage to a manageable level of +5V. For this, I went with the LM7805 step-down converter.

![Screenshot 2026-10-08 193701](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/4e44e75916859e4d6850b29a979ce3fb4cc053f35f23212e4c9aec28c69662d2.png)

Part 2: What I got accomplished on the PCB

So, I got lots done on the PCB. First, I found all of my parts (my sound, motor, and battery modules). This took me around an hour to scavenge for. Then, I added them in and routed everything together, which took me another hour. Clarifications for how are up above.

That's all I got accomplished today :)

### 2026-10-10 – Day 3: Starting the routing

**6h**

Day 3: Starting the routing

Ok, so today I did my most work yet: learning how to route and switching out a lot of parts. Learning to route was tough, and it's kept my PCB from being finished, but let's jump right in.

Part 1: Switching my parts

Originally, I had my capacitors and resistors chosen from the user-provided sources. This was great because the user-provided library has 1000s of options for me to choose from. Unfortunately, I decided to be dumb and not realize how tiny the real capacitors are. These capacitors are freaking less than a millimeter wide! I realized that me with my shaky hands and NO experience with soldering, let alone owning a pair of fine tweezers, was NOT going to be able to solder on something that tiny.

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 110658](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/5e429fb40b31c90bc801dadbed6e995c55bdff742965c4cb49fee5b45f3435c4.png)
(PS. The LSCS is the official vendor and partner of EasyEDA, the PCB software I use, and the user contributed is, well, it's in the name.)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/453ce0ca94fd1aabae10c0d0373ca1237d1dea3521b828253030e2691a5278e4.png)
(Sorry, centimeter, not millimeter. Still not ideal, though...)

Thankfully, EasyEDA clutched up, and I found out that their partner and manufacturer, JLCPCB, has parts in stock that they will solder on for you if they have them. So now I went on an hour-long quest to switch out my capacitors, resistor, voltage regulator, ceramic oscillator, and tactile switch with ones that they could provide (Technically, I could solder on the switches and voltage regulator, but I'm lazy, so I'm not doing all of that) So I switched my capacitors to the nice cermaic ones that JLCPCB rpovides (along with 1 electrolytic one), my switches to bigger 12x12 mm ones for easier use, my voltage regulator to a through hole one, and my cermic oscillator to a microscpoic littlun.

Part 2: Learning to route my PCBs

This part, like all of my learning sessions, definitely took the longest. I had to watch multiple videos on YT to understand the bare basics. To boil it down immensely:

- use the wire tool to connect different pins (called traces)
- bigger trace for the connections that need more power

I also researched the materials I should use for my PCB (wasted 30 minutes on that) before saying, "Yeah, Imma just do the beginner way and stick with copper." This video  (linked here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xEVntmYLARw) was extremely helpful, as it went really deep into the electrical engineering side of the concept and explained it very well. I highly recommend it if you are starting with PCB design like me.

To further learn the concept, I started messing around with my own design, seeing if I could connect stuff, and let me tell you, the dopamine I got from my 1st connection was a crazy hit. It was a very relaxing process before I realized that they had specific connection pins and had to get started for real this time.

Part 3: ROUTING

When I tell you routing frustrated the (bleep) out of me... genuinely, some (bleep) was going on. To start with, my software decided to render all of the components together in a nice neat rectangle. This LOOKS great and all, except IT'S NOT. That means that ALL of my components were shoved together, and that means that all of my traces would have been touching.

My 1st order of business was moving all of the parts outwards. This means I had to move all of my parts outwards, then the boundaries, test if it was OK, then it wasn't, and repeat. I did not want it to be too large because I am not trying to rack up the cost on just the PCB.

Once I got the boundaries just right, I started routing. Unfortunately, I do not have images of this because I forgot to save my work incrementally, but I will try to lay the scene. We have our microcontroller in the top-right corner, with ALL of the pins that connect to stuff facing away from the inside. Next, we have our motor module on the far left, again with ALL of the pins that may be necessary facing away. Great. Next, the switches were scattered, and the parts with the least amount of connections, the capacitors, were nice and neat in the center. Me being stupid, though, it was fine, and I started to route. I stopped routing after 30 minutes, after using over 40 vias (something that allows the trace to go from the top layer to the bottom layer to avoid intersecting other components' traces).

Next, I rearranged the parts and started routing again. I actually do have an image of this part:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/b394052c5da6120ba9c3167ddd650d2729f03cad16cbc272fd0607629aae7b0d.png)
Decently optimized, though I made minor changes later.

Routing is going great, actually. From here, it was pretty smooth sailing till I hit the ground connections. Clearly, I did not do enough research because I thought I had to connect all of them by wire. 30 minutes later, after some research, I figured out that I could just add a GND plate and connect everything to that. I applied the plate and all, when I decided that I should move 1 capacitor up, closer to the battery units. Rookie mistake. This took out a big chunk of my GND plate. I decided to do everything and finalize everything before applying the plate.

Now, it was decently easy. I just put all of the connections in, struggled for like an hour or two with placement for my net flags of 5V and BAT+, but I got there eventually, so I am decently proud of my work.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/ca302aabb212a807bf48741ace32c200f52f930b4e6c7c7cd3169686ac8d4f76.png)
(The ratlines you see are not negligible connections. All of that was GND, and all was connected. You can see the red dotted line surrounding it representing the GND plate, but I had it disabled for now.)

This is what made me mad. It looked beautiful. I had everything done. Finished. I decided to check over my schematic one more time before finalizing the design. I realized that I accidentally switched the connections for GND and a pin on my sound unit. No big problem. I quickly switched them and updated it. Then, I thought, "If I made one mistake, how many more did I make?"  I checked everything, and it actually looked great! Then I checked the motor unit and my heart sank.

You see, I had been using the 1x7 pin socket. This is a row of 8 pins sticking up, and a  ribbon cable will connect it to the module. Perfect for someone who doesn't trust himself with a soldering iron. However, the module I am using is not a 7-pin; it has 6. Worse, they are offset. And the final straw was that they had the pin connections different from what I had wired.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/2452f9c332673ad8008749020ff70b769c1e694cf9950565b89d8fef37172b2f.png)
(Left: socket. Right: MX1508 motor module)

I decided to switch itout and hope that I would not have to change too much. I was wrong.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/403d579d39f3554fee97c64e5eaaaac2a569cdbe6ba203cf81985d1814a37fee.png)

Now I have to reroute the entire board, but I guess I learned something.

That's all I did today!
